summary: This is an MDN Web Docs reference page for the JavaScript method RegExp.prototype.exec(), which executes a search for a match of a regular expression in a specified string and returns a result array or null. The page covers the syntax and parameter (str, coerced to a string), the return value's properties (index, input, groups, and the optional indices array when the d flag is set), and how lastIndex behaves with global or sticky flags. It also gives examples of successive matching and advises when test(), match(), matchAll() or search() are more appropriate; navigation and footer boilerplate were ignored.
one_line: MDN reference page describing JavaScript's RegExp.prototype.exec() method, its return value, lastIndex behavior, and examples.
key_facts: RegExp.prototype.exec() executes a search with a regular expression for a match in a specified string and returns a result array, or null.
The exec(str) parameter is the string to match; all values are coerced to strings, so omitting it or passing undefined searches for the string "undefined".
If the match fails, exec() returns null and sets the regex's lastIndex to 0.
If the match succeeds, the returned array has the matched text as its first item, followed by one item per capturing group.
The returned array has an index property, the 0-based index of the match in the string.
The returned array has an input property holding the original string that was matched against.
The groups property is a null-prototype object of named capturing groups, or undefined if no named capturing groups were defined.
The indices property is only present when the d flag (hasIndices) is set, and each entry is a two-element array giving the start and end index of a match or capturing group.
JavaScript RegExp objects are stateful when the global or sticky flags are set, storing a lastIndex from the previous match.
When using exec(), the global flag has no effect when the sticky flag is set; the match is always sticky.
exec() is the primitive method of regexps, and many other regexp methods such as @@replace call exec() internally.
If only a yes/no match is needed, RegExp.prototype.test() is recommended instead of exec().
The page's examples use the regex /quick\s(?<color>brown).+?(jumps)/dgi on the string "The Quick Brown Fox Jumps Over The Lazy Dog", giving index 4 and lastIndex 25.
The page's ECMAScript specification reference is sec-regexp.prototype.exec in the TC39 ECMA-262 specification.
The page was last modified on Sep 25, 2023.
